content.text: Now let me look at the Julia wrapper script and search for Epa/Epb/Epc in the traj-compression directory more thoroughly.

Now I have a comprehensive picture of the entire Fréchet distance computation in this codebase. Here are my findings:

---

## Fréchet Distance Computation in the Codebase

### 1. Where is the Fréchet Distance Computed?

The Fréchet distance is **not** computed inside the C++ `simplify` binary. Instead, the codebase delegates to an external Julia script.

**In `simplify.cpp`:**

- Line 445: `bool dist_flag = false;` — a flag set when `--dist` is passed.
- Line 980: When `--dist` is passed, the flag is set.
- Lines 1088–1092: After simplification, if `dist_flag && test_case_no != -1`, the code shells out to the Julia wrapper:

```1088:1092:simplify.cpp
if (dist_flag && test_case_no != -1) {
    std::filesystem::path frechet_path = repo_root / "scripts" / "frechet";
    std::string cmd1 = std::string("\"") + frechet_path.string() + "\" --in " + std::to_string(test_case_no) + " --path \"" + (repo_root / "data" / std::to_string(test_case_no) / "simplify.txt").string() + "\"";
    int rc = std::system(cmd1.c_str());
}
```

**In `scripts/frechet` (Julia):**

The script reads both the original and simplified curves, then calls `frechet_c_compute` from the `FrechetDist.jl` library:

```80:81:scripts/frechet
mw = frechet_c_compute(P, Q)
dist = Float64(mw.leash)
```

This computes the **continuous** Fréchet distance between the two polygonal curves.

**However, `simplify.cpp` also tracks its own expected upper bound.** The variable `expected_frechet` (line 699) accumulates the maximum squared distance from any disk center to any generated grid point:

```699:simplify.cpp
double expected_frechet = 0;
```

```701:717:simplify.cpp
std::vector<Point> get_points_from_grid(const Point &p) {
    // ...
    for_each_grid_row(px, py, [&](double px_, double py_,
                                  double y_actual, int x_min, int x_max) {
        for (int x = x_min; x <= x_max; x++) {
            points.emplace_back(px_ + x * GRID, py_ + y_actual);
            expected_frechet = std::max(expected_frechet, CGAL::to_double(CGAL::squared_distance(p, points.back())));
        }
    });
    return points;
}
```

This is printed at the end:

```965:simplify.cpp
std::cout << "Expected Frechet distance: " << std::sqrt(expected_frechet) << '\n';
```

This "expected Frechet" is a **theoretical upper bound** (see section 3), not an actual computed distance.

**There are no `Epa`/`Epb`/`Epc` types** anywhere in this codebase. The `Epeck`/`Epick` usage is about CGAL kernel selection (see next section).

---

### 2. Epeck vs Epick: How Chosen and Used

Defined in `simplify_geometry.h`, lines 11–12:

```11:12:simplify_geometry.h
using Epick = CGAL::Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel;
using Epeck = CGAL::Exact_predicates_exact_constructions_kernel;
```

Conversion functions are defined (lines 16–17):

```16:17:simplify_geometry.h
static inline CGAL::Cartesian_converter<Epick, Epeck> conv_to_exact;
static inline CGAL::Cartesian_converter<Epeck, Epick> conv_to_inexact;
```

**Epick is the default** (`simplify_geometry.h` lines 19–29):

```19:29:simplify_geometry.h
using Kernel = Epick;       // default
using Point  = Kernel::Point_2;
using Vector = Kernel::Vector_2;
// ... Polygon, Polygon_with_holes all use Kernel (= Epick)
```

**Epeck is used selectively** for one specific operation: segment-segment intersection inside the O'Rourke convex polygon intersection algorithm (`simplify.cpp`, lines 293–298, 319–344):

```293:298:simplify.cpp
// Pre-convert polygon vertices to Epeck once. The inner loop re-visits
// edges repeatedly, so amortizing the conversion cost across all seg_seg_int
// calls in this invocation reduces total overhead vs per-call conversion.
std::vector<Epeck::Point_2> Pe(n), Qe(m);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) Pe[i] = conv_to_exact(Pr[i]);
for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) Qe[i] = conv_to_exact(Qr[i]);
```

```319:344:simplify.cpp
auto inter = CGAL::intersection(
    Epeck::Segment_2(Pe[a1], Pe[a]),
    Epeck::Segment_2(Qe[b1], Qe[b]));
```

The comment explains why: "The inner loop re-visits edges repeatedly, so amortizing the conversion cost across all `seg_seg_int` calls in this invocation reduces total overhead." The code also pre-converts vertices to Epeck once upfront rather than per-call, further reducing overhead.

The O'Rourke path that uses Epeck is the fallback (called via `orourke_cgal::convex_intersect`), while the fast Sutherland-Hodgman path (`convex_intersect_fast`) uses only Epick throughout.

---

### 3. Theoretical Bound Formula

From the algorithm description in `report/report.typ` (line 47):

> For user-defined parameters **epsilon in (0, 1)** and **error bound delta > 0**, the algorithm constructs a simplified curve sigma that satisfies:
>
> **First guarantee (accuracy):** `d_F(sigma, tau[v_1, v_i]) <= (1 + epsilon) * delta`
>
> **Second guarantee (size):** `|sigma| <= 2 * opt - 2`, where `opt` is the minimum number of vertices to achieve Fréchet error at most `delta`.

The key relationship between `delta` and the desired Fréchet distance `D` is derived from the bound:

```
d = D / (1 + epsilon)
```

This is used in `benchmark.py` (lines 9–10 and 744):

```9:10:scripts/benchmark.py
- d = frechet_dist / (1 + e)
- Run simplify with delta=d, epsilon=e
```

```744:scripts/benchmark.py
delta = baseline_fret / (1.0 + eps)
```

---

### 4. Epsilon (e) Parameter Usage

Epsilon appears in three key formulas in `simplify.cpp`:

**Grid spacing** (lines 459, 661–679):

```459:simplify.cpp
double GRID_val() { return EPSILON * DELTA / (2 * SQRT2); }
```

```661:666:simplify.cpp
// Iterate every grid row y in [y_min, y_max] for which the disk
// of radius r = (1 + EPSILON/2) * DELTA has non-zero width.
template <class F>
static void for_each_grid_row(double px, double py, F &&f) {
    const double r = R_val();
    const double GRID = GRID_val();
```

The disk radius used in the algorithm (line 461):

```461:simplify.cpp
double R_val() { return (1.0 + EPSILON / 2.0) * DELTA; }
```

So epsilon controls:
- **GRID_val** = `EPSILON * DELTA / (2 * sqrt(2))` — the spacing of grid points approximating each error disk
- **R_val** = `(1 + EPSILON/2) * DELTA` — the radius of the disk used for grid approximation

---

### 5. Default Arguments for Epsilon and Delta

**Default values** in `simplify.cpp` (lines 456–457):

```456:457:simplify.cpp
double DELTA = 200;
double EPSILON = 0.6;
```

**Command-line overrides** (lines 981–986):

```981:986:simplify.cpp
else if (strcmp(argv[i],"-d") == 0 && i+1 < argc) {
    try { DELTA = std::stod(argv[++i]); } catch(...) { ... }
}
else if (strcmp(argv[i],"-e") == 0 && i+1 < argc) {
    try { EPSILON = std::stod(argv[++i]); } catch(...) { ... }
}
```

**CLI help text** (lines 472–473):

```
-d <delta>       Override DELTA (default 200)
-e <epsilon>     Override EPSILON (default 0.6)
```

There is **no default for the max distance "d"** in the sense of a separate parameter. `DELTA` serves this role. The relationship to the "true" Fréchet distance target `D` is `delta = D / (1 + epsilon)`, so if the target Fréchet distance is known (e.g., from a baseline algorithm), then `delta = D / 1.6` with the default epsilon of 0.6.

---

### Summary Table

| Item | Location | Details |
|---|---|---|
| **Fréchet distance computation** | `scripts/frechet` (Julia) | Calls `frechet_c_compute(P, Q)` from `FrechetDist.jl` |
| **Expected Frechet bound** | `simplify.cpp:699,713,965` | Upper bound via max squared distance to grid points |
| **Epick (default kernel)** | `simplify_geometry.h:11,19` | Used for all Point/Polygon/Vector operations |
| **Epeck (selective use)** | `simplify.cpp:293–344` | Used only for segment intersection in O'Rourke algorithm |
| **Epick ↔ Epeck conversion** | `simplify_geometry.h:16–17` | `conv_to_exact` / `conv_to_inexact` |
| **Accuracy bound** | `report/report.typ:47` | `d_F <= (1 + epsilon) * delta` |
| **Size bound** | `report/report.typ:47` | `|sigma| <= 2*opt - 2` |
| **Epsilon formula (grid)** | `simplify.cpp:459` | `GRID = EPSILON * DELTA / (2*sqrt(2))` |
| **Epsilon formula (radius)** | `simplify.cpp:461` | `R = (1 + EPSILON/2) * DELTA` |
